item.title: Spain sees widespread disruption in first general strike for 14 years
item.description:

Watch: Protesters gather across Spain for first general strike in 14 yearsByNick Beake, Europe correspondent, Reporting fromMadrid, Guy Hedgecoe, Reporting fromMadrid and Alba MorgadePublished11 November 2026, 14:06 GMTUpdated 3 hours ago
Transport and other public services across Spain have faced serious disruption in the first general strike for 14 years called by the main unions over housing and the high cost of living.
Demonstrations were also planned later on Wednesday, with the biggest protests expected in Madrid and Barcelona. Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November.
The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant."
However, the Spanish Confederation of Business Organisations said participation was "low and uneven", depending on the areas and sectors involved.
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
The general strike took place little more than two weeks ahead of national elections in Spain
Some of the biggest disruption on Wednesday was seen in the main industrial hubs of Madrid and the north-eastern region of Catalonia where traffic was halted on several main roads.
The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices.
The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later.

item.title: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
On Thursday Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will travel to Moscow and Dublin to hold talks with the Russian and Ukrainian presidentsByLaura GozziPublished2 hours ago
Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.
Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.
Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest."
"I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible.
Both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.
After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.
This latest round of talks had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.
For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member.
For Moscow, it is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion.
Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system.

item.title: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent relocated after alleged Iranian threats
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
The severity and nature of the threat against Scott Bessent remains unclearByBernd Debusmann JrWhite House reporter Published11 November 2026, 16:24 GMTUpdated 54 minutes ago
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his Washington DC home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, according to US media reports.
CBS, the BBC's US partner, said the relocation came after a photo of Bessent's home was published in the Wall Street Journal.
Bessent has been at the forefront of efforts to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and a wider economic blockade.
While the exact nature of the threats against Bessent remain unclear, US intelligence has warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans, including US officials.
"After the Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase," a source told CBS.
Georgetown is an affluent part of Washington that is home to a number of government officials and prominent residents.
Those security concerns, the source added, prompted authorities to move Bessent to a military base in the area.
In a statement, a Treasury Department spokesperson said only that Bessent "will not be deterred" by threats and "remains committed" to the US effort to pressure Iran's economy.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
In September, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans.
The New York Times has reported that the Iranian effort includes the targeting of current and former US officials. One source told the newspaper this has "reached a more advanced stage".

item.title: Schools in Italy, Scotland and Northern Ireland hit by threats in suspected bomb hoax
item.description:
Image source, Xinhua via ShutterstockImage caption,
These children had to leave their primary school in Rome as a result of one of the threats sent on WednesdayByPaul KirbyEurope digital editorPublished5 hours ago
Some 6,300 schools across Italy and more than 700 in Scotland and Northern Ireland have received bomb threats, according to local authorities.
In Italy a number of buildings were evacuated as a precaution but Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said checks so far had not indicated any evidence of "concrete danger".
"These reports appear rather linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern," she said on Facebook.
Scotland's education secretary Mairi McAllan said there was no risk to the public and specialist cyber-crime officers were working to identify the source of the messages. In Northern Ireland education officials told schools to remain open unless otherwise advised by police.
It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.
"As a parent and as a constituency MSP I understand just how concerning this will be for parents, for pupils, for carers and for school staff," McAllan said.
Scottish police had earlier said that the warnings were "immediately assessed" as hoaxes. However some local authorities confirmed that some schools had been evacuated.
"Our advice is that there is no requirement to evacuate schools or keep children away from education based solely on the content of the emails," Police Scotland said.
Italian officials said a single email appeared to have been sent on Wednesday to the inboxes of 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 state schools, and private schools were unaffected.
The message, said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan", caused alarm in many schools.
Italy's Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said the incidents were probably a "cyber-attack, not a genuine risk", adding that there appeared to be a clear strategy behind the rash of threats in across Europe targetin...

item.title: Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
The US removed all its bombers from the UK's RAF Fairford base last month after a major incident in September that police described as "suspicious"ByJack Burgess and Henry MoorePublished11 November 2026, 01:01 GMTUpdated 40 minutes ago
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe.
The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed.
The three men have been accused by the DOJ of being involved in 18 attacks and attempted attacks, including in London, Amsterdam and Paris. Some of the incidents were said to be directed by the men over FaceTime.
The DOJ said they acted in the name of the group Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI).
Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said.
The DOJ said that most recently, al-Hassani "orchestrated a terrorist plot" at RAF Fairford - where on 27 September a major incident was declared after suspicious vans were reported near the base.
Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident at RAF Fairford.
Iran has strongly denied any involvement.
Al-Hassani and Mohajeri were allegedly both in Iran at the time of the incident, the indictment claims.
Meanwhile, al-Saadi was coordinating with the pair through third parties from a prison in New York, where he is awaiting trial on previous charges after being arrested in August, it adds.

item.title: Kidnapper, 74, escapes from house arrest in Argentina by abseiling from balcony
item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Leonardo Bertulazzi was first arrested in Buenos Aires in 2002ByVanessa Buschschlüter, Latin America online editor and Paul Kirby, Europe digital editorPublished2 hours ago
A 74-year-old Italian man who was found guilty of a kidnapping carried out by a far-left militant group in the 1970s has escaped while under house arrest in Argentina and is on the run.
Leonardo Bertulazzi used a harness to abseil down from a fifth-floor balcony in the capital, Buenos Aires.
His escape was not immediately registered because he had tampered with his electronic ankle monitor so that it continued to transmit body temperature measurements even after he had prised it open and absconded.
Bertulazzi already spent decades as a fugitive after he was sentenced in absentia in Italy for the 1977 kidnapping of Italian naval engineer Pietro Costa.
He was awaiting extradition to Italy and was being monitored by the Argentine ministry of security through an ankle tag which registers the wearer's body temperature and movements.
Officials said that they had become suspicious when they noticed that the tag had remained stationary.
When they entered the fifth-floor apartment in the centre of Buenos Aires, Bertulazzi was gone, but the ankle monitor remained.
Wary of Bertulazzi's past with the Marxist guerilla group the Red Brigades and his bomb-making skills, police called in explosives experts in case it had been rigged to detonate, according to Argentine newspaper Clarín.
However, the experts found that while Bertulazzi had tampered with the device, he had done so to prevent the alarm from sounding once he removed it.
A nationwide manhunt is now under way.
Italian media say that his extradition to Italy had been imminent after his last appeal was rejected.
Bertulazzi was first arrested after using a false passport to cross into Argentina from neighbouring Chile in 2002.

item.title: Four grizzly bears killed in Canada after fatal attack on mother and daughter
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears are estimated to live in British Columbia (file image)ByDan WoodlandPublished11 November 2026, 13:17 GMTUpdated 4 hours ago
Four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with a fatal attack on a mother and daughter in the Canadian province of British Columbia.
Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going on an afternoon walk in a trail area in Bella Coola.
The British Columbia Conservation Office Service (BCCOS) launched an investigation into their deaths and forensic testing has since confirmed a sow and her three cubs were responsible for the attack.
All four were destroyed "in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines" to protect the public, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said in an update on Tuesday.
Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
Published6 days ago
"Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added.
The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare".
He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area.
The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found.

item.title: Vinícius Jr sends message to Sudan boy who received prosthetic legs after BBC report sparks appeal
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Watch: Vinícius Jr's surprise message to boy who received prosthetic legs after Sudan drone strikeByNawal Al-MaghafiSenior international investigations correspondent, Reporting fromCairoPublished11 November 2026, 00:19 GMT
In a dark room in Cairo, a 13-year-old boy looks up at a television screen, barely blinking.
The screen flickers and Real Madrid's superstar winger Vinícius Júnior appears addressing the young boy directly, in Arabic: "Zaher, mahaba" - Hello Zaher.
Zaher barely moves, his eyes wide, locked on his favourite footballer.
We first met Zaher a year ago in the ruins of Sudan's capital, Khartoum. He was a small quiet child, scarred by war - one of millions of children whose lives have been upended since the country's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) started fighting in 2023.
More than 17 million children are now in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan, according to the UN children's charity, Unicef. It says it has been able to verify that at least 4,300 have been killed or maimed, although it believes the true figure is far higher.
Zaher had lost both his legs in a drone strike. With little access to specialist treatment, he dreamed of the day he might walk and play football again.
More than a year later, as we walk into an apartment in the Egyptian capital, Zaher greets us with an enormous hug. His mother, Habibah, embraces us too.
Image source, Vinícius JúniorImage caption,
In his video message, Real Madrid star Vinícius Jr invited Zaher to watch a Real Madrid match together
The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs.
For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball aga...

item.title: Kenya discharges last Ebola patient in major milestone towards virus-free status
item.description:
Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Kenya has reported no new confirmed cases since 20 October 2026 ByWycliffe MuiaReporting fromNairobiPublished4 hours ago
Kenya has discharged its last Ebola patient - the seventh to recover from the virus - marking a major milestone in efforts to contain the disease in the East African nation, which now begins a 42-day countdown to officially being declared Ebola-free.
It had confirmed its first ever case of Ebola early in October when a Kenyan businessman died within days of arriving in the capital, Nairobi.
He had contracted the virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where more than 5,000 people have died in an ongoing outbreak that began in May. His mother also subsequently died.
Kenya's health minister said 135 identified contacts of the infected patients had also completed their 21 days in isolation.
"Today with the discharge of the last patient we can confirm and tell the world that seven patients have recovered - and all contacts have completed their follow-up monitoring," Aden Duale said.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) described it as an important achievement in the regional response to the outbreak.
"This is an encouraging moment for Kenya and for Africa. We must sustain surveillance and vigilance until the outbreak is officially declared over," Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya posted on X.
What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?
Published15 September
Kenya has reported no new confirmed cases since 20 October.
All the Kenyan cases were linked to the man who had travelled from DR Congo through Uganda, with health officials reporting no evidence of wider community transmission.
Those who have recovered following treatment included four healthcare workers.
Five patients were discharged on 3 November, followed by a sixth three days later, before the final patient was cleared on Wednesday.

item.title: Egyptian journalist's retrial adjourned as UN warns of 'assaults on press freedom'
item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Lina Attalah has said Egypt is "trying to limit the already-limited space" for independent mediaByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentPublished11 November 2026, 12:32 GMTUpdated 4 hours ago
A criminal court in Cairo has postponed the retrial of the prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah, whose case has drawn international condemnation.
Wednesday's opening hearing was adjourned until 18 November after defence lawyers representing the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr requested a new judge.
The UN has warned of "widening assaults on press freedom by Egyptian authorities, including the targeting, persecution and harassment of independent journalists".
Attalah told the BBC that a recent crackdown was meant to "send a chilling message" to "the very few newsrooms that are left".
She warned: "Everybody should be careful, everybody should be scared, everybody should be wondering if they are next."
Set up 13 years ago, Mada Masr became Egypt's leading independent news site with Attalah as its editor-in-chief and co-founder.
Last month, the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court convicted her of running a website without a licence - which she said she had tried in vain for years to obtain. She was issued a hefty fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds ($56,000; £42,000) and Mada Masr was ordered to shut down.
After that trial, Attalah found that a court had previously given her a one-year prison sentence, without her knowledge, for "spreading false news" - a charge often used against journalists and dissidents - as well as operating a website without a licence. It was issued in absentia in 2024, even though she was in the country at the time. Attalah is now being retried in that case by the same judge.
